generatedProse.concept-context: The School of Sport gives you plenty to revise actively across all three families. A visual mind map can link a coaching principle to the drills that develop it; reading a session rationale aloud exposes the gaps in your reasoning; and walking through the phases of a training session anchors their order. The strongest revision across the school combines families, because a model you can both diagram and explain aloud is one you can deploy under exam pressure.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students revise the same difficult topic: the stages of skill acquisition, with their several linked phases.

Tom makes one neat set of written notes and reads them over each day. The notes are accurate and tidy, but he never leaves one family: it is all reading. The cognitive, associative and autonomous stages blur together, because nothing forces him to reproduce the model or say it aloud. One passive technique, repeated, is still passive.

Amara draws the stages as a labelled sequence, then explains each one aloud into a recording, then lays a card for each stage around her desk and rehearses how a learner moves between them. Three techniques from three families, each demanding a different kind of production. The diagram fixes the sequence, the spoken version catches her gaps, and the physical layout anchors how a performer progresses. This is a varied, active approach.

Both revised the model for the same time. Amara chose techniques across families that matched the material, and ended with knowledge she could retrieve by more than one route.
generatedProse.summary: Active revision techniques in the School of Sport come in three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. You can now distinguish them and say what each suits, evaluate which turn a passive task active, and select a mix across families for a given topic. What unites the strong choices is production: rebuilding, explaining or enacting a model rather than merely reviewing it. The final lesson takes your prepared knowledge into the exam itself.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's revision more active than Tom's?

items.text: She used techniques from several families, each forcing her to produce the model in a different way.
She made neater and more accurate notes than Tom.
She spent longer revising than Tom.
She read her single set of notes more often.

feedback.correct: That's right. Drawing on several families, each demanding production, is what made it active.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about producing the model across more than one family.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara used techniques from several families, each forcing a different kind of production. Neater notes, more time or more re-reading would all have stayed passive.
